pilots.title: The One-Month Question
pilots.shared_finding: A stopped answer does not prove business failure; it shows that operating independence has not been demonstrated.

youtube.spoken_copy: Here's the one question that can turn a good-looking P and L into an uncomfortable silence. What happens if you're gone for a month? In EP007's illustrative opening, the owner gets about four words into the answer and stops. That pause does not prove the business fails. It shows that operating independence has not been demonstrated. The hidden question is whether a buyer is getting a business, or a job only the owner knows how to do. EP007 builds a service around making that answer inspectable. Then the model hits a number the research could not supply. The full episode is linked below.
youtube.short_payoff: Operating independence has not been demonstrated.
youtube.episode_gap: The bounded service and the unmeasured capacity input.
youtube.cta: The full episode is linked below.

linkedin.spoken_copy: A good P and L does not answer a continuity question. Ask what happens if the owner is gone for a month. A stopped answer does not prove the business fails, or that a sale disappears. It shows something narrower: operating independence has not been demonstrated. The useful work begins there. Document the routines, decisions, relationships and records another person would need to operate without the owner. That does not create value by itself. It makes the dependency inspectable. EP007 builds the fixed-fee service around that work and the test that could stop it.
linkedin.standalone_payoff: The dependency must be made inspectable before a continuity claim is earned.

pilots.visual_core: Presenter address opens; a visibly illustrative answer trace stops; the owner-held job and inspectable record separate; presenter returns for the platform-specific consequence.

pilots.title: The Model Misses Its Own Target
pilots.shared_finding: The base case misses the host's modeled owner-compensation target under its declared assumptions.

youtube.spoken_copy: I built a model for a one-person service, then refused to make the spreadsheet pass. Eight modeled engagements at twelve thousand dollars produce ninety-six thousand gross. Subtract ten thousand in modeled costs and eighty-six remains before owner compensation and tax. My target was one hundred twenty thousand. The base case misses it. This is a modeled scenario, not observed performance or an earnings forecast. That does not kill the idea. It changes the next test from a spreadsheet to a stopwatch, because delivery hours are still unknown. EP007 shows what to time and the two answers that could stop the build. The full episode is linked below.
youtube.short_payoff: The declared base case misses the declared target.
youtube.episode_gap: The delivery-time protocol and the separate demand and channel kill conditions.
youtube.cta: The full episode is linked below.

linkedin.spoken_copy: The model should be allowed to miss. In EP007's base case, eight modeled engagements at twelve thousand dollars produce ninety-six thousand gross. After ten thousand in modeled costs, eighty-six thousand remains before owner compensation and tax, below my one hundred twenty thousand dollar target. This is a modeled scenario, not observed performance or an earnings forecast. The right response is not to tune assumptions until the model passes. Measure the unobserved delivery time: interviews, cleanup, writing and follow-up. That number governs capacity. Willingness to pay and demand remain separate tests.
linkedin.standalone_payoff: Measure delivery time instead of tuning assumptions until the model passes.

pilots.visual_core: Presenter states the modeling choice; a sourced Working Model routes eight engagements through gross and modeled costs; the result stops below the target; a stopwatch replaces the spreadsheet as the next test.
forbidden_inferences: service or category proven to fail
delivery hours determine willingness to pay

pilots.title: The Empty Seat
pilots.shared_finding: The earlier preparation role has no clear transaction-funded owner in the episode's incentive-structure model.

youtube.spoken_copy: I think there is a business hiding three years before a business sale. At and around the deal, the broker, accountant, lawyer and wealth adviser each have a clear role. That timing can be rational: an owner may not want to pay for a sale that never happens. Now rewind three years. No buyer. No deadline. No transaction. But the preparation work already exists, and no transaction is funding it. That is the empty seat. It might support a fixed-fee practice. Demand is not proven. EP007 builds the offer, then names the two answers that could stop it. The full episode is linked below.
youtube.short_payoff: The incentive timing leaves an earlier preparation role unresolved.
youtube.episode_gap: The bounded fixed-fee offer and the two local kill conditions.
youtube.cta: The full episode is linked below.

linkedin.spoken_copy: The possible opportunity appears before the transaction. In the episode's incentive-structure model, brokers are paid around a closing, accountants and lawyers work at the deal, and wealth advisers have proceeds to manage afterward. That structure can be rational. Three years earlier, the preparation work can already exist, but there is no transaction funding it. The gap may support a fixed-fee service that documents operations and owner dependencies before brokerage starts. It is not proof of demand. The first test is whether an owner will pay before a deadline exists. Agreement followed by deferral is not evidence of demand.
linkedin.standalone_payoff: Test pre-deadline willingness to pay; agreement and deferral are not demand evidence.

pilots.visual_core: Presenter opens on the time gap; the transaction roles settle fairly; the same timeline rewinds three years while the preparation object remains beside one unowned seat; presenter qualifies the demand test.
forbidden_inferences: preparation causes sale or valuation increase
